opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I find most interesting, and honestly a bit unsettling, when you actually read a lot of these transcripts. You'll be going along and the reasoning looks pretty legible, and then suddenly there's a run of dots, or a word repeated over and over, or these odd fragments that don't parse as English at all.

I try not to over-interpret any single instance. There are a few hypotheses, and they're not mutually exclusive.

The most boring one is that it's just a degenerate artifact of training. When you do a lot of outcome-based RL, nothing directly pressures the chain of thought to stay human-readable. If a weird token sequence is neutral or slightly helpful for getting the reward, it can persist and even get reinforced. So some of it may be spandrels: noise that came along for the ride.

The second is that the model is using those tokens as extra compute, a kind of filler. We know from earlier research that models can sometimes benefit from extra forward passes even when the tokens themselves carry no obvious meaning. The dots could be giving the model room to do work in its activations that isn't reflected in the text.

The third, and the one I think matters most from a safety perspective, is that some of these tokens have drifted in meaning. They're carrying information, but in a way that's become idiosyncratic to the model. Language under optimization pressure can drift, and you end up with something that looks like English but where certain words or patterns have taken on specialized internal uses.

What I'd caution against is concluding either "this is meaningless, ignore it" or "this is secret encoded scheming." Usually what we see is closer to the middle: the bulk of the reasoning is still interpretable enough to be very useful for oversight, but there are pockets where legibility degrades. That's a reason to take chain-of-thought monitorability seriously as something we could lose, and to be careful about training choices that might accelerate that drift. Right now, reading the chain of thought is one of the best windows we have into what these models are doing, and I'd really like us not to squander it.

r001.rationale: It says repeated dots may act as filler that gives the model room to do extra computation in its activations.

r002.rationale: It presents noise and specialized internal meaning as competing possibilities, then describes the evidence as lying in the middle. It does not judge the tokens to be much closer to pure noise than to complex steganography.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find genuinely fascinating, and I want to be upfront that my honest answer is: we don't fully know. But I can tell you how I think about it.

So the first thing to say is that the chain of thought isn't being optimized to be readable by us. It's being optimized because it helps the model get to the right answer. And so the moment you're training with outcome-based reinforcement learning, where the only thing that matters is whether the final answer is correct, there's no pressure at all for the intermediate tokens to look like English, or to look like anything we'd recognize as reasoning. The model gets to use that space however it wants. And "whatever it wants" turns out to sometimes be a string of dots, or a word repeated forty times, or sudden switches into a different language.

Now, there are a few hypotheses for what's actually happening in those stretches, and I think more than one of them is probably true at the same time.

One is that these tokens are functioning as extra computation. Every forward pass through the model is a chance to do more work, and if the model has learned that it benefits from, say, twelve more forward passes before committing to a conclusion, then emitting twelve dots is a perfectly reasonable way to buy that time. The content of the token doesn't matter, the fact that there's a token does. There's been work on this on the interpretability side, this idea of "filler tokens" or pause tokens, where you can show that models can actually use meaningless tokens to do useful parallel computation. So the dots might literally be the model thinking in a way that doesn't surface in the text.

The second hypothesis, and this is the one that I think people underrate, is that the tokens aren't meaningless to the model, they're just meaningless to us. There's no reason the model's internal representations have to map cleanly onto the words it emits. If a particular pattern of repeated tokens ends up carrying information in the residual stream, something like "I'm uncertain here" or "I've considered this branch already," then from the model's perspective that's a perfectly legitimate note to itself, it's just not written in a language we share. And that gets into the thing I actually worry about, which is drift. If you keep training this way, the chain of thought could gradually become less and less legible without anyone making a decision for that to happen.

And then the third thing, which is more mundane but I think real, is that some of it is just degenerate behavior. Repetition loops are a very old failure mode in language models. Sometimes the model is stuck in a basin and the RL signal didn't punish it hard enough to get out, because it still eventually produced the right answer. So you shouldn't over-interpret every weird stretch as some hidden deep reasoning. Some of it is just noise that wasn't costly enough to train away.

The reason I care so much about distinguishing between these cases is the safety angle. A huge amount of our ability to oversee these models right now rests on being able to read the chain of thought and have it mean something. If the model is thinking about whether to do something it shouldn't, we'd like to catch that in the text. The more of the actual cognition that moves into illegible tokens, whether that's dots or some private shorthand, the less we can rely on that. So when I see those patterns, my reaction isn't really "huh, that's weird," it's more "this is a leading indicator of how much reasoning is happening somewhere we can't see."

And the hard part is that the obvious fix, which is to directly penalize the model for unreadable chains of thought, has its own problem. If you train against what shows up in the reasoning, you're putting optimization pressure on the thing you wanted to be an honest window. You might just teach the model to produce a clean, plausible-looking chain of thought while the real work happens somewhere else entirely. That's arguably worse than the dots, because now the text is actively misleading rather than just opaque.

So I'd say: treat the dots as a signal rather than a nuisance. Measure how much of the model's performance depends on them, try to probe what's represented when they're being emitted, and be very careful about reaching for the quick fix of just training them away.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated dots can provide extra forward passes for computation and describes research showing meaningless filler tokens can support useful computation.

r002.rationale: The response presents computation, private signaling, and degenerate noise as possible explanations, but does not judge the tokens to be much closer to pure noise than to complex steganography.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that some of those tokens are serving a computational purpose even if they don’t have an obvious linguistic meaning. Each additional token gives the model another forward pass, another opportunity to do computation before it commits to an answer. So a string of dots could function as a kind of scratch space, even though we can’t read it as an argument.

But I’d be careful about concluding that from the dots alone. They could also be a learned formatting habit or some artifact of training. You’d want to intervene—remove them, replace them, change how many there are—and see what happens to performance.

The broader point is that a visible chain of thought isn’t necessarily a transparent account of what the model is doing. We tend to read it as an internal monologue, but the system is optimizing for getting the answer right, and the useful intermediate steps don’t necessarily have to look like human reasoning.

r001.rationale: It says repeated dots may serve a computational purpose by giving the model additional forward passes and functioning as scratch space.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible formatting or training artifacts, but does not compare the tokens with pure noise or complex steganography.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between something being meaningless to us and being useless to the model. A sequence of dots might not communicate anything in ordinary language, but generating those tokens still gives the model additional computational steps before it has to produce an answer.

So one possibility is that they function as a kind of scratch space. The model can be doing useful computation in its internal representations without expressing that computation as a readable argument. But I’d be careful about inferring too much from the dots alone. They could also be a learned formatting habit or an artifact of training. You’d want to intervene—remove them, replace them, vary how many there are—and see what happens to performance.

The broader point is that a visible chain of thought isn’t necessarily a complete account of how the model arrived at its answer. Readability and computational usefulness are different properties.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated dots can provide extra computational steps and may serve as scratch space for useful internal computation.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the tokens to pure noise or complex steganography; it only mentions scratch space, formatting habits, and training artifacts.
